title: Harvesting courgettes
subtitle: Picking at the right size, handling gluts, and ending the season
excerpt: Courgettes should be cut while still young, at 10 to 15 cm long, before they become marrows. Picking every two to three days at peak season is essential; a courgette left to swell into a marrow tells the plant to stop producing. Gluts in July and August can be roasted, frozen, or given away.
sourceNotes: RHS courgette growing guide (rhs.org.uk). Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), kitchen garden section. USDA cooperative extension notes on summer squash production, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: The yellow trumpet-shaped flowers of the courgette plant. Male flowers (on a thin straight stalk) open first and for longer than female flowers (which sit directly at the base of a tiny courgette). Both are edible; stuffed and fried male flowers are a classic use. Removing male flowers for eating reduces pollination briefly but does not significantly reduce crop yield on a healthy plant with multiple flowers open.

content.text: The rule for courgettes is simple: check the plant every two days and pick every fruit under 15 cm. A courgette doubles in size in 48 hours in warm weather; a fruit you ignored on Tuesday will be a marrow by Thursday. The
at the end of each courgette often remain attached when picked; they are edible and signal the fruit is fresh.

Cut the stalk cleanly with a knife or sharp secateurs; never pull, which can damage the stem and introduce rot. Leave a short stalk on each courgette; this extends shelf life. Handle gently; courgette skin marks and bruises easily. Pick in the morning if possible, before the heat of the day softens the flesh.

At peak season in July and August, two courgette plants can produce more than a household can use. Roasted courgette freezes well: cut into 2 cm slices, toss with oil, roast until golden, cool, and freeze in portions. Use for pasta, soup, or frittata through autumn. Very large courgettes that become marrows can be stuffed and baked, or hollowed and used as the base for a simple gratin.

Courgette plants are killed by frost. Clear by mid-October; pull up the whole plant and put it on the compost unless it showed signs of mildew or rot. If you want to save seeds, leave one fruit to mature fully into a marrow on the plant through the season; extract the seeds in autumn, dry, and store for next year.
